prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock based on magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms, and its realisation at a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18

statement.case_for: I keep B001 alone, with Katori and Ye, as in round 1; my configuration has not changed. After reading all eight statements I tested the case against the criteria I apply. Is it an original discovery or invention? The magic-wavelength lattice is a distinct physical idea, since it lets many neutral atoms be interrogated at once with the light shift cancelled, and it is not a faster or neater version of the comb or of single-ion clocks. Is it experimentally verified? Yes: several independent laboratories reproduce uncertainties near 10^-18 and compare clocks across sites, so the result does not rest on one group. Does it open a door? Yes: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, bounds on varying constants and dark-matter couplings, and the technical basis for redefining the second. Can we be absolutely sure of who did the original work? For the two ideas that define the citation, the proposal and first realisation of the lattice (Katori) and the route to 10^-18 with many-body and systematic control (Ye), the record described in the eight statements is consistent. I recommend a citation that names the lattice concept and its realisation, so that it does not claim optical clocks in general and does not overlap the 2005 and 2012 citations. I would not add a second part this year: no member put one in a preferred configuration, and each alternative carries a named credit or timing problem.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is still that the committee may see this as a refinement of areas honoured in 2005 and 2012. My answer is that the lattice principle is distinct, but this is a judgment and it has not been settled by evidence. Second, the 10^-18 figure is a result in systematic control, which is closer to a record than to a discovery about nature, so the citation should rest on the invention of the lattice scheme and use the precision as the demonstration, not as the discovery. Third, the two-name credit leaves out Lemonde, Ludlow, Bloom, Hinkley, Campbell and the Paris, NIST/Boulder and PTB teams, who made decisive contributions. Nobody on the committee, myself included, has independently verified the priority record for the magic-wavelength proposal and the first strontium experiments, and I regard that as a real gap in a committee that must be sure of the original work. Finally, the SI second has not yet been redefined, though I now agree with the colleagues who treat that as a decision that follows the physics.

responses.point: Danielsson says the refinement objection is answered by a citation that stresses the lattice-clock concept and its consequences instead of clock accuracy alone, and that the SI redefinition should not hold the prize back.
responses.response: I accept both points and have changed my own wording accordingly. In round 1 I left the SI redefinition as an open timing question; I now think he is right that it is a metrological decision that follows the physics and that the prize does not need to wait for it, since the discovery and its verification are already in hand. I would go one step further on the citation than he does. His wording says the clock opens new tests of fundamental physics, which is true, but I would keep that out of the citation itself, because those tests are consequences still being exploited and a citation should honour what was done. I prefer to name the invention of the lattice scheme and its realisation at 10^-18, and leave the applications to the popular and scientific background.

responses.point: Kroll names B042 and B003 as alternatives and says the road from record uncertainty to broad scientific use is long and that the new-physics payoff has not yet been demonstrated.
responses.response: I agree that the new-physics payoff is not yet demonstrated: the bounds on varying constants and dark-matter couplings are limits, not discoveries. That is why I do not want the citation to rest on them. It also bears on the second part he lists as an alternative. B042 needs three names from five, and the committee has not agreed which three; I do not see how a theory and experiment split among Bloch, Cirac, Greiner, Zoller and Esslinger can be made without leaving out someone whose original work is as strong as those credited. I would not add it this year. On B003 I share his view that it is too close to the 2025 prize and has an unresolved fourth name.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, stresses that independent laboratories reproduce and compare lattice clocks across sites, so the calibration and systematics work has been done by the community and not only by the discoverers; he also admits relying on recollection for the priority of the early experiments.
responses.response: His first point is the strongest answer to my own worry about 10^-18 being a record. Cross-site comparisons mean the number is a checked property of nature and of the atoms, and that is what I mean by verification. On the second point, I share the gap. The chair's question about priority is the right one, and none of us can resolve it from memory. I suggest we rely only on what is clearly documented: the magic-wavelength proposal and first strontium lattice clock are Katori's, and the route to 10^-18 with spin-polarised fermions and systematic control is Ye's. If anyone on the committee or an external expert can show that another group's contribution to the first of these is of the same standing, I would want to hear it before the vote and I would reconsider the two-name credit.

responses.point: Eriksson moved from B010 first to B001 and openly asks whether his move reflects a wish for consensus more than his own judgment of merit, and keeps B010 and B017 as alternatives.
responses.response: I put the same question to myself, because I also moved from B015. The test I used was whether I would choose B001 if the support counts were hidden, and my answer is yes, on the grounds above: original idea, independent verification, and a new capability. I think his caution is the right one and I would encourage him to apply it to B010 too. I respect his scientific case for topological insulators, but he himself says that credit among Kane-Mele, Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang, Fu-Kane-Mele and Hasan is genuinely split, and a three-name cap cannot represent that. I do not agree with ranking it ahead of B001 for a prize this year. I keep B017 as an alternative because it provides a new tool for controlling quantum phases, but the pairing mechanism is open and the experimental credit (Cao, Dean, Efetov, Young) is wider than the credited names.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as a distinct discovery or invention and not a refinement of the 2005 and 2012 prizes; I judge it distinct but cannot prove it.
The unverified priority record for the magic-wavelength proposal, the first strontium lattice clock and the first 10^-18 result across Katori, Ye and the Paris, NIST/Boulder and PTB groups.
Whether a two-name credit is defensible against the contributions of Lemonde, Ludlow, Bloom, Hinkley and Campbell, which a three-name cap might partly address only by choosing among equals.
For the alternatives, whether B017 will be mature once the pairing mechanism is understood, and whether B015 should honour the 1995 discovery or the MgO step.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B001, B017, B015 or any other shortlisted candidate. None of the credited names appears among my listed co-authors or mentors. My field is electron microscopy, not atomic physics, so I rely on the other members' accounts of the clock priority record. I note that Johansson has said he should recuse himself from B003, which I do not propose in any case.
